claims.text: High-temperature mechanical strength in single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys is chiefly governed by edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Thermoelastic stability is chiefly governed by edge-dislocation-mediated plasticity and grain-boundary interactions.
Decreasing grain size increases grain-boundary area.
The increased grain-boundary area in finer-grained specimens amplifies edge-dislocation pile-up and boundary-related interactions.
Grain refinement produces higher initial yield strength than a coarse-grained baseline of the same composition.
Finer-grained specimens undergo more rapid or pronounced high-temperature softening than coarser-grained specimens.
At elevated temperatures, edge dislocations dominate plastic deformation in BCC refractory high-entropy alloys.
At elevated temperatures, edge dislocations accumulate at grain boundaries and thereby dominate plastic flow.
Edge-dislocation behavior influences high-temperature strength retention.
In situ diffraction can resolve temperature-dependent lattice strain and elastic-modulus behavior in a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Finer-grained specimens will exhibit greater edge-dislocation activity near grain boundaries than coarser-grained specimens.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys at temperatures of at least 1000 °C.
Evolution of secondary phases at extreme temperatures could invalidate the proposed edge-dislocation and grain-boundary mechanism.
Prolonged thermal exposure may alter microchemistry or phase stability and consequently change dislocation behavior.
